chapter.name: Thermodynamics
chapter.blurb: The chapter develops the laws governing the interconversion of heat, work and internal energy for bulk systems. It introduces thermal equilibrium and the Zeroth Law, the First Law with specific heat capacities and the special thermodynamic processes, and the work done in each. It ends with the Second Law, reversible and irreversible processes, and the Carnot engine, whose efficiency depends only on the temperatures of its two reservoirs.

scope_in.item: Describe thermodynamics as a macroscopic science that specifies the state of a system by measurable macroscopic variables (pressure, volume, temperature, mass, composition), and distinguish it from mechanics, which deals with the motion of a body as a whole
State what an equilibrium state is in thermodynamics, distinguish adiabatic and diathermic walls, and describe how two systems reach thermal equilibrium
State the Zeroth Law of Thermodynamics and use it to arrive at temperature as the quantity that is equal for systems in thermal equilibrium
Define internal energy as the sum of molecular kinetic and potential energies (excluding the kinetic energy of the system as a whole) and explain that it is a state variable
Distinguish heat and work as two modes of energy transfer that are not state variables, and identify which mode operates in a given situation

State the First Law, Delta Q = Delta U + Delta W, with Delta Q the heat supplied to the system and Delta W the work done by the system, apply it with correct signs, and explain the path dependence of Delta Q and Delta W
Use Delta W = P Delta V for work against a constant pressure, including the worked example of the vaporisation of water
Define heat capacity, specific heat capacity and molar specific heat capacity with their units, and calculate heat from them
Recall that the molar specific heat capacity of solids is about 3R (Table 11.1, carbon an exception), the definition of the calorie, 1 cal = 4.186 J and the specific heat capacity of water
Explain why a gas has two specific heats and state, use and derive C_p - C_v = R for an ideal gas
Explain state variables and equilibrium states, use the ideal gas equation of state PV = mu R T, and classify variables as extensive or intensive
Describe a quasi-static process and why it is an idealisation

Define isothermal, isobaric, isochoric and adiabatic processes (Table 11.2) and calculate the work done in an isothermal process, W = mu R T ln(V2/V1), and in an isobaric process, W = P(V2 - V1) = mu R (T2 - T1)
Apply the First Law to isochoric and cyclic processes, and find the work done from a pressure-volume description of a process (Exercise 11.8)
Use P V^gamma = constant, gamma = C_p/C_v and T V^(gamma - 1) = constant for an adiabatic process of an ideal gas, and calculate the adiabatic work W = mu R (T1 - T2)/(gamma - 1)
State the Kelvin-Planck and Clausius statements of the Second Law and recognise processes that the First Law allows but the Second Law forbids
Define reversible and irreversible processes, give examples, and state the two causes of irreversibility and the conditions for reversibility
Describe the four steps of the Carnot cycle, and use eta = 1 - Q2/Q1 = 1 - T2/T1 and Q1/Q2 = T1/T2 with temperatures in kelvin
State Carnot's theorem and outline the argument for it; describe the reversed Carnot cycle as a reversible refrigerator

concepts.name: Thermodynamic description, thermal equilibrium and the Zeroth Law
concepts.description: Thermodynamics as a macroscopic science, the meaning of an equilibrium state, adiabatic and diathermic walls, thermal equilibrium, and the Zeroth Law, which leads to the concept of temperature.
concepts.idea: Thermodynamics describes a bulk system by a few measurable macroscopic variables, and two systems that stop exchanging heat through a conducting wall share one common property, their temperature.
concepts.rule: Thermodynamics is a macroscopic science: the state of a gas is specified by variables such as pressure, volume, temperature, mass and composition, not by the motion of individual molecules, and it is concerned with the internal macroscopic state of a body, not its motion as a whole. A system is in an equilibrium state if the macroscopic variables that characterise it do not change in time. An adiabatic wall is an insulating wall that does not allow heat to flow; a diathermic wall is a conducting wall that allows it. Two systems separated by a diathermic wall change until there is no more energy flow between them: they are then in thermal equilibrium and their temperatures are equal. Zeroth Law: two systems in thermal equilibrium with a third system separately are in thermal equilibrium with each other, so if T_A = T_C and T_B = T_C then T_A = T_B.
concepts.example: A cup of milk and a steel spoon have each been left in the same refrigerator until neither changes any more. Each is in thermal equilibrium with the air of the refrigerator, so by the Zeroth Law the milk and the spoon are in thermal equilibrium with each other: they are at the same temperature.

questions.q: Two gases A and B are held in separate rigid containers of fixed volume, and the pair is insulated from everything else by adiabatic walls. At first the wall between them is adiabatic, and the pressures stay at P_A = 2.0 atm and P_B = 1.0 atm. The wall between them is then replaced by a fixed diathermic wall; the pressures drift to 1.8 atm and 1.1 atm and then stay steady. Explain (a) why nothing changed at first, (b) why the pressures changed after the wall was replaced although the volumes did not, and (c) what is equal for A and B at the end, and whether their pressures need to be equal.
questions.a: (a) An adiabatic wall does not allow heat to flow, so any state of A is in equilibrium with any state of B and nothing changes. (b) A diathermic wall lets energy (heat) flow from one gas to the other, so their macroscopic variables change until equilibrium is reached; the containers are rigid, so the volumes are fixed and only the pressures can change. (c) At the end A and B are in thermal equilibrium, so their temperatures are equal. Their pressures need not be equal (here they are 1.8 atm and 1.1 atm): thermal equilibrium means equal temperature only.
s: (a) Adiabatic wall allows no heat flow, so any pair of states can coexist
(b) Diathermic wall allows heat flow, so the states change; volumes are fixed by the rigid containers, so only the pressures change
(c) Temperatures are equal at the end; the pressures need not be equal

questions.a: In mechanics, equilibrium means that the net external force and the net external torque on a system are zero. In thermodynamics, a system is in an equilibrium state if the macroscopic variables that characterise it (such as pressure, volume, temperature, mass and composition) do not change in time.
s: Mechanics: net external force and torque on the system are zero
Thermodynamics: the macroscopic variables characterising the system do not change with time

questions.q: Four systems P, Q, R and S are studied. P is in thermal equilibrium with Q, and Q is in thermal equilibrium with R. When R and S are joined through a diathermic wall, heat flows from S to R. (a) Deduce how the temperatures of P, Q, R and S compare. (b) State, with a reason, what happens if P and S are joined through a diathermic wall. (c) State what happens if P and S are instead separated by an adiabatic wall.
questions.a: (a) By the Zeroth Law, T_P = T_Q and T_Q = T_R give T_P = T_Q = T_R. Heat flows from the body at higher temperature to the one at lower temperature, so T_S > T_R; hence S is hotter than P, Q and R. (b) Since T_S > T_P, heat flows from S to P through the diathermic wall and their states change until the two temperatures become equal (thermal equilibrium). (c) An adiabatic wall allows no heat flow, so the states of P and S stay as they are, although their temperatures differ.
s: T_P = T_Q = T_R by the Zeroth Law, and T_S is higher because heat flows from S to R
Diathermic wall: heat flows from S to P until their temperatures are equal
Adiabatic wall: no heat flows and the states of P and S remain unchanged

questions.q: A student claims: 'If two gases are in thermal equilibrium with each other, they must have the same pressure and the same volume.' Evaluate this claim.
questions.a: The claim is wrong. Thermal equilibrium requires only that there is no net flow of heat between the systems, which means that their temperatures are equal. Two gases in different containers can be at the same temperature while having quite different pressures and volumes; pressure and volume are separate variables of each gas.
s: Judgement: the claim is wrong; thermal equilibrium requires equal temperature only
Reason: pressures and volumes of the two gases can differ while the temperatures are equal (no heat flow)

questions.q: Devise a thought experiment, using three gas systems and the two kinds of wall, that could test the Zeroth Law of Thermodynamics. Describe the arrangement in two stages and state the observation that would confirm the law.
questions.a: Stage 1: keep systems A and B separated from each other by an adiabatic wall, and put each of them in contact with a third system C through a conducting (diathermic) wall. Wait until the states stop changing, so that A and B are each in thermal equilibrium with C. Stage 2: now insulate C from A and B with an adiabatic wall, and replace the adiabatic wall between A and B by a conducting wall. Observation: if the states of A and B do not change any further, A and B were already in thermal equilibrium with each other, which is what the Zeroth Law states: two systems in thermal equilibrium with a third system separately are in thermal equilibrium with each other.
s: Stage 1: A and B kept apart by an adiabatic wall while each is brought to thermal equilibrium with C through a conducting wall
Stage 2: C is insulated from A and B, and A and B are connected through a conducting wall
Confirming observation: the states of A and B do not change further, so they are in thermal equilibrium with each other

concepts.name: Heat, internal energy and work
concepts.description: Internal energy as the energy of the random motion of the molecules and a state variable, and heat and work as two distinct modes of energy transfer that are not state variables.
concepts.idea: A system possesses internal energy; heat and work are not possessed but are two ways in which energy passes into or out of the system.
concepts.rule: Internal energy U is the sum of the kinetic and potential energies of the molecules of a system in the frame in which its centre of mass is at rest; the kinetic energy of the system as a whole is not included. If intermolecular forces are neglected, U of a gas is the sum of the kinetic energies of the random translational, rotational and vibrational motion of its molecules. U is a state variable: it depends only on the state of the system, not on how that state was reached. Heat is energy transfer due to a temperature difference between the system and the surroundings; work is energy transfer brought about by other means, such as moving a piston. Heat and work are modes of energy transfer, not state variables: 'a gas in a given state has a certain amount of heat' is meaningless, while 'a certain amount of heat is supplied to the system' is meaningful. Heat flows from the body at higher temperature to the one at lower temperature.
concepts.example: The air in a balloon can be warmed by leaving the balloon in sunlight (heat, because of a temperature difference) or by squeezing the balloon (work). Either way the internal energy of the air rises, and afterwards the state of the air does not show which of the two was used.

questions.q: Distinguish between the heat supplied to a system and the internal energy of the system.

It is a mode of energy transfer, not something the system contains, and it is not a state variable.
s: Internal energy: energy of the molecules of the system, a state variable with a definite value in each state

questions.q: Two samples of the same gas have the same mass. Sample 1 was first heated and then compressed; sample 2 was first compressed and then heated. Both end at the same pressure, volume and temperature. (a) Compare the internal energies of the two samples. (b) Can one tell, from the final state alone, which sample was supplied with more heat? (c) What does this show about heat and work compared with internal energy?
questions.a: (a) The internal energies are equal: the internal energy of a given mass of gas depends only on its state (pressure, volume, temperature), and the two final states are the same. (b) No. The final state does not record how it came about, so the amounts of heat supplied and work done cannot be read from it; they can be different for the two samples. (c) Internal energy is a state variable, while heat and work are not: they are modes of energy transfer that depend on the process, and only their effect, the change in internal energy, belongs to the state.
s: (a) Equal internal energies, because U depends only on the state
(b) No: the final state does not show how much heat or work was involved
(c) U is a state variable; heat and work are modes of energy transfer and are not state variables

questions.q: A student says: 'A cylinder of gas carried in a fast train has more internal energy than an identical cylinder in the same state at rest in the laboratory, because it has extra kinetic energy.' Evaluate this statement.
questions.a: The statement is wrong. Internal energy includes only the energy associated with the random motion of the molecules, reckoned in the frame in which the centre of mass of the system is at rest. The kinetic energy of the cylinder as a whole is not part of the internal energy, so the two cylinders, being in the same state, have the same internal energy.
s: Judgement: wrong; the two cylinders have the same internal energy
Reason: the kinetic energy of the system as a whole is not included in U, which counts only the random molecular motion

questions.q: Devise two different procedures for raising the temperature of water in a beaker from 20 degrees C to 30 degrees C, one that uses only heat and one that uses only work. Then explain what the two procedures together show about heat, work and internal energy.
questions.a: Heat only: place the beaker in contact with a hotter body (for example a hot plate or a flame); energy flows into the water because of the temperature difference. Work only: insulate the beaker and stir the water vigorously with a paddle (or rub or shake it); the work done on the water raises its internal energy with no temperature difference involved. The final state of the water, at 30 degrees C, is the same in both cases, so the increase in internal energy is the same. This shows that heat and work are two different modes of transferring energy to a system, while internal energy is a property of the state that does not depend on which mode was used.
s: A valid heat-only procedure: contact with a hotter body
A valid work-only procedure: mechanical work such as stirring, with the water insulated
Conclusion: same final state and same change in U, so heat and work are modes of transfer while U is a state variable

concepts.name: The First Law of Thermodynamics
concepts.description: The first law as energy conservation, Delta Q = Delta U + Delta W, with the book's sign convention, the path dependence of heat and work, and the work P Delta V done against a constant pressure.
concepts.idea: The heat supplied to a system is shared between raising its internal energy and doing work on the surroundings; nothing is lost.
concepts.rule: Delta Q = Delta U + Delta W, where Delta Q is the heat supplied TO the system by the surroundings, Delta W is the work done BY the system ON the surroundings and Delta U is the change in internal energy of the system. Q > 0 means heat is added to the system and Q < 0 that heat is removed; W > 0 means work is done by the system and W < 0 that work is done on it. Delta U depends only on the initial and final states, while Delta Q and Delta W depend on the path; the combination Delta Q - Delta W = Delta U is path independent. If Delta U = 0 then Delta Q = Delta W. For a gas in a cylinder with a movable piston, the work done by the gas against a constant pressure P is Delta W = P Delta V, so Delta Q = Delta U + P Delta V.
concepts.example: A gas is supplied with 250 J of heat and does 90 J of work on the surroundings: Delta U = Delta Q - Delta W = 250 J - 90 J = 160 J, so its internal energy rises by 160 J.

concepts.name: Specific heat capacity and the relation C_p - C_v = R
concepts.description: Heat capacity, specific and molar specific heat capacity, the value 3R for solids, the calorie and the specific heat of water, and the two specific heats of an ideal gas with C_p - C_v = R.
concepts.idea: The heat needed for a given temperature rise depends on the substance, on its amount and on the conditions under which the heat is supplied.
concepts.rule: Heat capacity S = Delta Q / Delta T. Specific heat capacity s = (1/m) Delta Q / Delta T, unit J kg^-1 K^-1; molar specific heat capacity C = (1/mu) Delta Q / Delta T, unit J mol^-1 K^-1, where mu is the number of moles. C depends on the nature of the substance, its temperature and the conditions under which heat is supplied, not on its amount. For a solid, energy considerations give C = 3R, which agrees with measured values at ordinary temperatures for most solids (carbon is an exception). One calorie is the heat needed to raise the temperature of 1 g of water from 14.5 degrees C to 15.5 degrees C; 1 cal = 4.186 J, and the specific heat capacity of water is 4186 J kg^-1 K^-1. For an ideal gas the molar specific heats at constant pressure and at constant volume satisfy C_p - C_v = R.
concepts.example: A 0.50 kg block of a metal with specific heat capacity 380 J kg^-1 K^-1 is warmed by 20 K: Delta Q = m s Delta T = 0.50 x 380 x 20 = 3800 J.

concepts.name: State variables, equation of state and quasi-static processes
concepts.description: Equilibrium states and state variables, the ideal gas equation of state, extensive and intensive variables, and the idealised quasi-static process.
concepts.idea: Only equilibrium states can be described by state variables, so thermodynamics imagines processes slow enough for the system to pass through equilibrium states all the way.
concepts.rule: Every equilibrium state of a system is completely described by the values of its state variables (for a gas: pressure, volume, temperature, mass, and composition for a mixture). A gas expanding freely into vacuum or an exploding mixture is not in an equilibrium state. The relation between the state variables is the equation of state; for an ideal gas PV = mu R T, so for a fixed amount of gas only two variables are independent. The P-V curve for a fixed temperature is an isotherm. Extensive variables indicate the size of the system (internal energy U, volume V, mass M) and are halved when an equilibrium system is divided into two equal parts; intensive variables (pressure P, temperature T, density rho) are unchanged. A quasi-static process is an infinitely slow process in which the system stays in thermal and mechanical equilibrium with its surroundings throughout, the pressure and temperature of the surroundings differing only infinitesimally from those of the system.
concepts.example: 3 mol of an ideal gas at 500 K in a vessel of volume 0.0415 m^3, with R = 8.3 J mol^-1 K^-1: P = mu R T / V = 3 x 8.3 x 500 / 0.0415 = 3.0 x 10^5 Pa.

concepts.rule: Isothermal: temperature constant; for an ideal gas PV = constant (Boyle's law), Delta U = 0, and the heat absorbed equals the work done by the gas, Q = W = mu R T ln(V2/V1), positive for expansion (heat absorbed) and negative for compression (heat released). Isochoric: volume constant; no work is done, and the heat absorbed goes entirely to change the internal energy and temperature. Isobaric: pressure constant; W = P (V2 - V1) = mu R (T2 - T1), and the heat absorbed goes partly to increase the internal energy and partly to do work. Cyclic: the system returns to its initial state, so Delta U = 0 and the total heat absorbed equals the work done by the system. For any quasi-static process the work done by the gas is the sum of P Delta V over the process.
concepts.example: A gas expands at a constant pressure of 1.5 x 10^5 Pa from 2.0 x 10^-3 m^3 to 5.0 x 10^-3 m^3: W = P (V2 - V1) = 1.5 x 10^5 x 3.0 x 10^-3 = 450 J of work done by the gas.

concepts.name: The adiabatic process
concepts.description: A process with no heat exchange: the relation P V^gamma = constant for an ideal gas, the ratio gamma of the specific heats, the work done, and the accompanying change of temperature.
concepts.idea: With no heat entering or leaving, any work a gas does must come out of its own internal energy, so an adiabatic expansion cools the gas and an adiabatic compression warms it.
concepts.rule: In an adiabatic process the system is insulated from the surroundings and the heat absorbed or released is zero, so by the First Law the work done by the gas equals the decrease in its internal energy. For an ideal gas P V^gamma = constant (quoted without proof), where gamma = C_p / C_v is the ratio of the specific heats (ordinary or molar) at constant pressure and at constant volume; so P1 V1^gamma = P2 V2^gamma. Combined with the ideal gas equation this gives T V^(gamma - 1) = constant. The work done by the gas in going from (P1, V1, T1) to (P2, V2, T2) is W = (P2 V2 - P1 V1) / (1 - gamma) = mu R (T1 - T2) / (gamma - 1). If W > 0 (work done by the gas) then T2 < T1; if W < 0 (work done on the gas) then T2 > T1.
concepts.example: An ideal gas with gamma = 1.5 is compressed adiabatically to one-ninth of its volume. Pressure: P2 = P1 x 9^1.5 = 27 P1. Temperature: T2 = T1 x 9^0.5 = 3 T1.

concepts.name: The Second Law of Thermodynamics; reversible and irreversible processes
concepts.description: Why a second law is needed, its Kelvin-Planck and Clausius statements, the definition of a reversible process, and the causes of irreversibility in natural processes.
concepts.idea: Conservation of energy does not decide which way a process runs; the Second Law does, and it makes the spontaneous processes of nature irreversible.
concepts.rule: The Second Law disallows many processes that are consistent with the First Law. Kelvin-Planck statement: no process is possible whose sole result is the absorption of heat from a reservoir and the complete conversion of the heat into work. Clausius statement: no process is possible whose sole result is the transfer of heat from a colder object to a hotter object. The two statements are equivalent. The law implies that the efficiency of a heat engine can never be unity. A process is reversible if it can be turned back so that both the system and the surroundings return to their original states with no other change anywhere in the universe. A process is reversible only if it is quasi-static and there are no dissipative effects. Spontaneous processes of nature are irreversible, for two main causes: many processes take the system through non-equilibrium states (free expansion, explosive chemical reaction), and most processes involve friction, viscosity and other dissipative effects.
concepts.example: A hot cup of coffee left on a table cools to room temperature. The reverse, the coffee warming up again by taking heat from the cooler room with nothing else changing, would conserve energy but is never observed: it would violate the Clausius statement, so the cooling is irreversible.

questions.a: The First Law would be satisfied: the table could convert some of its internal energy into an equal amount of mechanical energy of the book, which would rise to a height at which its potential energy equals that energy, so energy would be conserved. Yet this is never observed. It is forbidden by the Second Law of Thermodynamics, which disallows many processes that are consistent with the First Law.
s: Energy is conserved: internal energy of the table becomes an equal amount of mechanical energy of the book, so the First Law allows it
It never happens: the Second Law of Thermodynamics forbids it

questions.q: A hot metal block at 400 K is joined by a conducting rod to a cold block at 300 K, and heat flows from the hot block to the cold one. Analyse why this process is irreversible by considering (a) whether it is quasi-static, (b) what its exact reversal would require, and (c) what a reversible transfer of heat would need instead.
questions.a: (a) It is not quasi-static: there is a finite temperature difference (100 K) between the bodies exchanging heat, whereas a quasi-static process allows only an infinitesimal temperature difference between the system and what it exchanges heat with. (b) Exact reversal would require the same heat to pass from the cold block back to the hot block with no other change anywhere, which is the transfer of heat from a colder to a hotter object as the sole result and is forbidden by the Clausius statement. (c) A reversible transfer must be quasi-static and free of dissipative effects: heat must pass between bodies whose temperatures differ only infinitesimally.
s: (a) Finite temperature difference, so the process is not quasi-static
(b) Reversal means heat passing from colder to hotter with no other effect, violating the Clausius statement
(c) A reversible transfer needs an infinitesimal temperature difference (quasi-static) and no dissipative effects

questions.q: A student argues: 'The free expansion of a gas into an evacuated space is reversible, because we can always push the gas back into its original volume with a piston.' Evaluate this argument.
questions.a: The argument is wrong. A process is reversible only if both the system and the surroundings can be returned to their original states with no other change anywhere in the universe. Pushing the gas back restores the volume of the gas, but it requires work from the surroundings (and the heat produced has to be removed), so the surroundings are left changed. The free expansion is therefore irreversible.
s: Judgement: wrong; reversibility requires the system AND the surroundings to be restored with no other change anywhere
Compressing the gas back needs work from the surroundings, which are therefore not restored; so the free expansion is irreversible

questions.q: Design a way of expanding a gas from volume V to volume 2V at a fixed temperature that is as nearly reversible as possible. Then describe two changes to your design that would make the expansion irreversible, one for each of the two main causes of irreversibility.
questions.a: Nearly reversible design: hold the gas in a cylinder with a frictionless movable piston, in thermal contact with a large reservoir at the fixed temperature, and reduce the load on the piston in extremely small steps (for example by removing grains of sand one at a time), so that the expansion is quasi-static and the gas stays in equilibrium with the surroundings at every stage. Irreversible change 1 (non-equilibrium states): remove the load suddenly, or let the gas expand freely into an evacuated space; the gas then passes through non-equilibrium states. Irreversible change 2 (dissipative effects): use a piston that rubs against the cylinder wall, so that work is dissipated by friction.
s: Reversible design: quasi-static (very slow, small steps, in contact with a reservoir at the fixed temperature) with a frictionless piston
A change that takes the gas through non-equilibrium states, such as a sudden or free expansion
A change that introduces a dissipative effect, such as friction at the piston

concepts.name: The Carnot engine and its efficiency
concepts.description: The reversible engine working between two temperatures, the four steps of the Carnot cycle, its efficiency 1 - T2/T1, the relation Q1/Q2 = T1/T2 and Carnot's theorem.
concepts.idea: The best possible engine between two reservoirs is a reversible one, and its efficiency is fixed by the two temperatures alone.
concepts.rule: A Carnot engine is a reversible engine operating between a hot reservoir (source) at temperature T1 and a cold reservoir (sink) at temperature T2. The Carnot cycle consists of two isothermal processes connected by two adiabatic processes: (1 to 2) isothermal expansion at T1 absorbing heat Q1; (2 to 3) adiabatic expansion in which the temperature falls from T1 to T2; (3 to 4) isothermal compression at T2 releasing heat Q2; (4 to 1) adiabatic compression back to T1. Efficiency eta = W/Q1 = 1 - Q2/Q1 = 1 - T2/T1, with the temperatures in kelvin; also Q1/Q2 = T1/T2. Carnot's theorem: working between two given temperatures, no engine can have an efficiency greater than that of the Carnot engine, and the efficiency of the Carnot engine is independent of the nature of the working substance. Run in reverse, the cycle is a reversible refrigerator, taking heat Q2 from the cold reservoir, having work W done on it and delivering heat Q1 to the hot reservoir.
concepts.example: A Carnot engine works between reservoirs at 750 K and 300 K: eta = 1 - T2/T1 = 1 - 300/750 = 0.6.

s: Q2 = 1000 J, from Q1/Q2 = T1/T2 or from the efficiency

A Carnot engine uses 1 mol of an ideal gas and works between reservoirs at 500 K and 300 K. In the isothermal expansion at 500 K the volume of the gas doubles, and in the isothermal compression at 300 K the volume is halved. Take R = 8.3 J mol^-1 K^-1 and ln 2 = 0.70. (b) In the isothermal compression, Q2 = mu R T2 ln(V3/V4) = 1 x 8.3 x 300 x 0.70 = 1743 J (equivalently Q2 = Q1 x T2/T1 = 2905 x 300/500). (c) W = Q1 - Q2 = 2905 - 1743 = 1162 J, which agrees with eta = 1 - 300/500 = 0.4 and W = 0.4 x 2905 J.
s: Q1 = mu R T1 ln 2 = 2905 J
Q2 = 1743 J, from mu R T2 ln 2 or from Q1 T2/T1

questions.q: A Carnot engine works between 600 K and 400 K. An engineer can either raise the temperature of the hot reservoir by 100 K or lower the temperature of the cold reservoir by 100 K. Compare the two efficiencies obtained (to two decimal places) and say which change is better.
questions.a: Raising the hot reservoir to 700 K: eta = 1 - 400/700 = 0.43. Lowering the cold reservoir to 300 K: eta = 1 - 300/600 = 0.50. Lowering the temperature of the cold reservoir gives the higher efficiency, so it is the better change (the original efficiency is 1 - 400/600 = 0.33).
s: eta = 0.43 with the hot reservoir at 700 K
eta = 0.50 with the cold reservoir at 300 K, so lowering the cold reservoir temperature is better

questions.q: In a Carnot cycle with mu moles of an ideal gas, the volume changes from V1 to V2 in the isothermal expansion at T1 and from V3 to V4 in the isothermal compression at T2, and V3/V4 = V2/V1. By adding the work done by the gas in the four steps, show that the two adiabatic steps contribute nothing in total, and hence obtain the efficiency of the engine.
questions.a: Isothermal expansion at T1: W(1 to 2) = Q1 = mu R T1 ln(V2/V1). Adiabatic expansion: W(2 to 3) = mu R (T1 - T2)/(gamma - 1). Isothermal compression at T2: work done on the gas = Q2 = mu R T2 ln(V3/V4). Adiabatic compression: work done on the gas = mu R (T1 - T2)/(gamma - 1). Total work by the gas W = W(1 to 2) + W(2 to 3) - W(3 to 4) - W(4 to 1); the two adiabatic terms are equal and opposite and cancel, leaving W = mu R T1 ln(V2/V1) - mu R T2 ln(V3/V4). With V3/V4 = V2/V1, W = mu R (T1 - T2) ln(V2/V1). Efficiency eta = W/Q1 = (T1 - T2)/T1 = 1 - T2/T1.
s: Writes the work (heat) in the two isothermal steps: mu R T1 ln(V2/V1) and mu R T2 ln(V3/V4)
Shows that the two adiabatic works, each mu R (T1 - T2)/(gamma - 1), are equal and opposite and cancel
Uses V3/V4 = V2/V1 to get eta = W/Q1 = 1 - T2/T1

questions.q: An inventor claims that his engine, working between reservoirs at 800 K and 400 K, absorbs 1000 J of heat from the hot reservoir in each cycle and delivers 600 J of work. Evaluate the claim.
questions.a: The claim cannot be true. The maximum possible efficiency between these reservoirs is that of a Carnot engine: eta = 1 - T2/T1 = 1 - 400/800 = 0.5, so at most 0.5 x 1000 = 500 J of work can be obtained per cycle. The claimed engine has efficiency 600/1000 = 0.6, which is greater than the Carnot efficiency, and no engine operating between two temperatures can be more efficient than the Carnot engine.
s: Carnot efficiency = 0.5, i.e. at most 500 J of work from 1000 J
Claimed efficiency 0.6 exceeds the Carnot value, so the claim is impossible

questions.q: Design a Carnot engine that has an efficiency of 0.25 and delivers 500 J of work in each cycle. Choose suitable temperatures (in kelvin) for the two reservoirs, find the heat absorbed and the heat released per cycle, and verify that your values satisfy Q1/Q2 = T1/T2.
questions.a: Efficiency 0.25 requires 1 - T2/T1 = 0.25, i.e. T2/T1 = 0.75; for example T1 = 400 K and T2 = 300 K. Heat absorbed: Q1 = W/eta = 500/0.25 = 2000 J. Heat released: Q2 = Q1 - W = 2000 - 500 = 1500 J. Check: Q1/Q2 = 2000/1500 = 4/3 and T1/T2 = 400/300 = 4/3, so the values are consistent.
s: Reservoir temperatures in kelvin chosen with T2/T1 = 0.75
Verifies Q1/Q2 = T1/T2 for the chosen temperatures
